column2: Power system

The most important part for the safety of your boards. By the end of this part you have three measured voltage sources: 5 V for the brain and body, 5 V for the camera, and 6 V for the motors and servos.
Four power rules
Every converter is adjusted and measured with no load. New converters often come out with the same voltage as the input (8 V), and that is enough to destroy an ESP32.
22 AWG power wires use only these three colors. 5 V wires use 26 AWG red-black. The converter modules and the BMS have no reverse polarity protection.
Change wiring only when the main switch is off. If anything gets hot, smokes or smells, switch it off and pull the cells.
Two 18650 cells can deliver tens of amps if shorted. Never let the plus and minus wire ends touch.
Two skills you will use constantly
Using the multimeter
Your multimeter. The black lead always goes in the COM socket.

DC voltage (V symbol with a straight line): red lead in the VΩmA socket, turn to 20 in the V⎓ area. Black probe to minus, red to plus. A negative number means the probes are reversed; it does no harm.
Continuity (tone/diode symbol): with power OFF, touch the two probes to two points. A beep = directly connected.
Resistance Ω: to confirm a resistor value, for example a 2k reads about 1.98-2.02 kΩ.
Never measure voltage with the red lead in the 10A socket. That socket is almost 0 Ω, so touching it to a battery is the same as a short circuit. The 10A socket on this multimeter also has no fuse.
Your soldering iron, 0.8 mm solder, RMA-223 flux and desoldering braid.
Heat the iron for 2-3 minutes. Clean the tip, then coat it with a little solder so it is shiny.
Apply a little flux to the spot you will solder. Flux makes the solder flow evenly.
Touch the iron tip to the pad and the leg together for 1-2 seconds, then touch the solder to the pad (not to the iron tip). Remove the solder first, then the iron.
A good joint is a small shiny cone. Dull or ball-shaped = a "cold joint"; reheat it.
Solder bridging two pins? Lay the braid on top, heat it, and the solder is absorbed.
Do not breathe in the flux smoke. Work near a window or a fan.
Plug the pin header into the breadboard first, rest the module on top, then solder. The breadboard keeps the pins upright. Solder one pin first, check that the module sits flat, then do the rest.

Strip 5-8 mm, slide the heat shrink on first, twist the two ends together, solder, then slide the heat shrink over the joint and heat it with the side of the iron or a lighter (do not let it burn). Cut the heat shrink to about 2 cm from the 40 mm stick.
Your Taffware heat shrink
26 AWG wire, servo wires, capacitor legs
Two 22 AWG wires, motor wires
Three or four wires at once (midpoint + 4.2V, servo joint + capacitor)
Switch and fuse legs
Choose a size that can still slide over the joint; after heating it shrinks to about half. Black for GND, red for plus so the wire ends are easy to recognize.
Build the power system
Work in order. Every stage has a success sign before you move on to the next.
Check both 18650 cells
Your two 18650 cells. Treat them as one pair.

Why this way? The two cells are wired in series, so the same current passes through both. The emptier cell runs out first and the BMS cuts power sooner. Starting from two matched cells lets both last a long time.
Both cells between 3.0 and 4.2 V, and they differ by less than 0.1 V. A freshly full cell reads about 4.15-4.2 V.
OK to lock in Nothing is installed at this stage. It is only a check.
Not yet Do not solder or put the cells into the holders yet. Always use these two cells as a pair.
If it does not work
Reads below 2.5 V: the cell is too empty. Do not use it in the robot.
Reads 0 V: check the probes are in the right sockets (COM and VΩmA) and the dial is on V⎓, not V~.
Cut the wires and solder them to the BMS
Your BMS pads. The 充电/放电 text beside ⊕ ⊖ means "charge/discharge".
Seen from above, the positions match the robot exactly (see the layout drawing in Part 6). The numbers in the drawing = the numbers in the table and in the steps.

Why this way? The BMS cuts the minus line (⊖) if a cell is too empty, too full, or the current is too high. The 4.2V pad is used to measure and balance each cell, so the current is small and a thin wire is enough. Your BMS spec: 10 A continuous, 20 A peak, short-circuit protection. The BMS's low-voltage cutoff is wide (2.3-3.0 V per cell), so the robot must still switch itself off earlier at around 3.3 V per cell (6.6 V total) using the battery ADC. The cells are charged in the iMFG charger (4.2 V per cell), not through the BMS.
Two wires (4.2V and P−) attached firmly (a gentle tug does not pull them off), and no solder bridges two pads.
OK to lock in The solder joints of the 4.2V wire (yellow heat shrink) and P− on the BMS pads. The lengths were calculated from the final position in the robot, so these are final connections.
Not yet The ⊕, 8.4V and 0V pads are still empty (Stages 3 and 4). The BMS is not strapped to the top plate yet: that is Part 6 Stage 3.
Wire the two holders and insert the cells
Your two holders. The spring end = − (black wire), the flat plate end marked + = + (red wire).
Holder, BMS and wire number positions: the level-2 map in Stage 2. Connection order: 0V first, then the midpoint, then 8.4V. Disconnect in the reverse order.
P+ to P− reads 7.4-8.4 V. During this, the ⊕ pad and the P− wire must not touch.
OK to lock in The holder solder joints to the 0V pad, the midpoint (heat shrink already covering it) and the 8.4V pad.
Not yet The holders are not bolted to the top plate yet (Part 6 Stage 3). Both cells are taken out again in Stage 4 before soldering the fuse.

P+ to P− reads 0 V even though 0V to 8.4V is correct: the BMS protection is latched (common when cells are first installed). Remove both cells, wait 10 seconds, insert cell 1 and then cell 2 again. If it is still 0 V, with P+ and P− connected to nothing, briefly touch a piece of wire between the ⊖ pad and the 0V pad to "wake up" the BMS. Still 0 V: check that the 0V and 8.4V wires are not swapped.
Total voltage about 0 V or only one cell: the midpoint joint came loose, or one cell is reversed. Remove the cells and check the + marks.
Anything gets hot when the cells go in: remove the cells at once. There is usually a short circuit or a reversed cell.
Install the fuse, main switch and battery WAGO
The fuse holder and blade fuse.
The rocker switch. Check the maximum current printed on its body.
Why this way? The fuse is placed as close to the battery as possible, so that if a wire is stripped and shorts anywhere after it, the fuse blows before the wire burns.
The switch really breaks and makes the plus rail, the fuse sits between the BMS and the switch, and WAGO + / WAGO − read 7.4-8.4 V with the switch ON.
OK to lock in All the fuse and switch solder joints with heat shrink closed over them, and the plus rail and P− wires in WAGO + and WAGO − (lever closed, a gentle tug does not pull them out).
Not yet The fuse, switch and WAGO are not strapped to the plate yet. The empty holes in the WAGO are deliberately left for the converters and capacitor.
Wires come out of the WAGO easily: the strip is not long enough or the lever is not fully closed. Strip exactly 11 mm, push in until it stops, close the lever until it clicks, then tug gently.
Adjust LM2596 #1 to 5.0 V (logic rail)
1 IN+ plus input (from the battery plus rail). 2 IN− minus input (GND rail). The VIN+ and VIN− text is on the PCB.
3 OUT+ 5 V output. 4 OUT− minus output.
5 Blue trimpot: turn it with a small flat screwdriver to set the output voltage. It takes a dozen or more turns for a big change.
6 Button: switches the display between input voltage (IN LED lit) and output (OUT LED). 7 Voltmeter display. This display is approximate; trust the multimeter.

Why this way? The LM2596 is a buck converter: it chops the battery voltage quickly and then smooths it, so it is far more efficient than an ordinary regulator. The output must be slightly above what the ESP32 needs (5 V input), but no more than 5.5 V.
The multimeter reads 4.95-5.1 V from OUT+ to OUT−, and it stays the same after switching off and on.
OK to lock in The 5.0 V setting of LM2596 #1: do not turn the trimpot again. The WAGO + and WAGO − wires to IN+ and IN−.

Not yet The module is not mounted on the level-1 plate yet (Part 6 Stage 2). OUT is only connected to the 30P board and the S3 in Part 6 Stage 6; before that the DevKit and S3 run from USB (Stage 8 uses it only for the LED test).
The voltage does not change even after dozens of turns of the trimpot: turn it the other way. This trimpot has no noticeable end stop.
Output equals input (about 8 V): the trimpot is still at its maximum. Keep turning in the direction that lowers the voltage.
Adjust the XL4015 to 6.0 V (motor and servo rail)

1 and 2: two screw terminals. IN and OUT are printed on the underside of the board. Usually the input is on the side of the 100 µF 50 V capacitor (5) and the output on the side of the 220 µF 35 V capacitor. Flip the board over and read the labels before connecting.
3 and 4: two trimpots. One sets the voltage (CV), one limits the current (CC). Which is which, we find in step 4.
OUT+ to OUT− reads 5.9-6.1 V with no load.
OK to lock in The 6.0 V setting of the XL4015 (do not turn the voltage trimpot again, do not change the current-limit trimpot) and the OUT wires to WAGO 6V and WAGO −6.
Not yet The XL4015 is not mounted yet: its place is on level 2 (Part 6 Stage 3). Its input wires are deliberately long because they must climb up to level 2.
Later, when the motors run, the voltage drops a lot and a red LED lights on the XL4015: the current limit (CC) is too low. Turn the CC trimpot a few turns clockwise, then check again.
Adjust LM2596 #2 to 5.0 V (camera rail)
Output 5.0 V. A separate camera rail keeps the camera's WiFi current spikes from disturbing the ESP32-S3.
OK to lock in The 5.0 V setting of LM2596 #2 and the WAGO + and WAGO − wires to IN+ and IN−.
Not yet The module is not mounted on the plate yet. Its OUT is only connected to the camera in Part 4 Stage 3.
Test each rail with a small load
Why this way? A 330 Ω resistor limits the LED current to about (5 - 2) / 330 = 9 mA. Without a resistor, the LED burns out immediately.
The LED lights on both rails and the voltage does not change. You now have a safe power source for all three boards.
OK to lock in The whole power system is electrically final: voltage settings, solder joints and the contents of the WAGOs. Do not change them again.
Not yet Mounting to the chassis waits until the dry stack in Part 6 Stage 1 passes. The battery and modules may still be lifted and moved.

Table mode and run mode
Table mode (USB to laptop)

Used when uploading code and reading the Serial Monitor. The boards get power from USB. The red 5 V wire from the LM2596 to the board is unplugged, but the GND wire stays connected. The motors and servos may still get power from the XL4015.
Run mode (battery)

USB unplugged, the red 5 V wire plugged into the expansion board's 5V pin. Never plug in USB and the 5 V wire from the LM2596 at the same time: two slightly different 5 V sources fight each other, and current can flow back into the laptop's USB port.
To make it easy, use a dedicated female jumper wire (for example red) for the 5 V to each board. That is the only wire you plug and unplug when switching modes.
How to charge the battery
iMFG 2-slot charger: 5 V input, 4.2 V 1 A output per cell.
Switch off, and take both cells out of the holders.
Put them in the charger with the + facing the way the slot marks show. Plug the charger into your 5 V 2 A adapter.
Wait until the light shows full. Charge near you, on a surface that does not burn easily, and do not leave it while you sleep.
Measure: each cell about 4.15-4.2 V. Put them back in the holders in the order cell 1 then cell 2.
Always use the same two cells as a pair. If you later get a third cell, keep it as a spare and do not mix it in.
For long storage (more than a month), keep around 3.7-3.8 V per cell, in a cool place.
